title: Why You Must Stop Giving Fake Grades
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin contends that inflated, unearned grades have become rampant, driven by pandemic-era pressure to show recovery, a view that objective standards are discriminatory, and performance levels so low that honest grading would fail huge numbers of students. He argues none of these justifications hold up, because grade inflation ultimately harms the very students it claims to protect. He details three consequences: students eventually face a reckoning they are unprepared for, they come to believe a false story about their own abilities that collapses painfully later, and they simply learn less because they are never confronted with the true gap in their skills. His prescription is to keep instruction, support, and encouragement strong while holding grading standards fixed, letting students experience real failure and disappointment as the only reliable trigger for genuine change and resilience.
points: Grade inflation is driven by pandemic pressure, fears that standards are discriminatory, and widespread low performance.
Inflated grades eventually collide with reality — in college, the workplace, or beyond — with no groundwork laid to cope.
Students who believe false praise about their abilities are devastated when the truth becomes unavoidable later.
Inflating grades means students learn little academically because they're never shown how far behind they actually are.
The fix is to keep support and instruction excellent while holding standards fixed in cement, letting real failure teach resilience.
quotes: Teachers giving grades students haven’t earned is rampant, staggering in its increasing frequency.
The result is that an ‘A’ for one student can look very different from an ‘A’ given to another.
The bill will eventually come due. A person can only fake what is falsely written down on paper for so long.
They’re so pumped full of praise and phony appraisal of their abilities that when the truth sets in it’s devastating. Their whole world is upended. Their dreams die.
They have no grit, no toughness, no resiliency. They’ve been given excuses for so long that that’s all they have.
But set your standards in cement. Let your students fail if that’s where they fall. Let them feel disappointment.
It is in the face of hard truth that change happens. It is confrontation with being knocked down that provides the purchase to begin standing back up.
